checks.label: The square of any side of a triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides minus twice the product of the other two sides and the cosine of the included angle: at every whole angle of the hinge from 0° to 180°, the third side measured off the drawing, squared, is 9 + 16 − 24 cos C, the c² bar stands exactly that high on the bars' scale, it is the first bar and the correction together, and the side's label and the bar's label agree

It helps to know it's the Pythagoras Theorem with something extra so it works for all triangles: at 90° the hinge shows a right-angle square and the label Pythagoras, the correction is 0 and c = 5, and at every other whole angle from 0° to 180° the correction is not zero and neither the square nor the label is shown

Sine, cosine and tangent all have different positive or negative values depending on what quadrant they are in: at every whole angle, the cos C readout is negative exactly when the tip of arm a is left of the hinge, past 90°, and then the correction bar stands above the zero line, solid; below 90° the readout is positive and the bar hangs below the line, dashed, with its key

The terminal side of the angle intersects the circle at the point (x, y), which is equivalent to (cos t, sin t): on the screen that builds the rule, arm a is lesson 3's arm made 3 times longer, so at every angle it can be dragged to, its tip measured off the drawing is 3 cos C across and 3 sin C up from the hinge, and the dashed gap to the end of arm b is 4 − 3 cos C across and 3 sin C up

The cosine rule is a formula used to find a missing side or angle in a triangle when two sides and included angle, or all the lengths of all three sides, are known: from sides 3, 4 and 6 it gives cos C = −0.458 and C = 117.3°, and the hinge opened to that angle draws a third side of exactly 6; from two sides and the angle between them it gives the side, 3.61 at 60°

The sine rule can find a side from another side and two angles or an angle from two sides and a non-included angle: in the drawn triangle with A = 40°, B = 60° and a = 5, side b measured off the drawing is 5 × sin 60° ÷ sin 40° = 6.74, and on the swing arm, with b = 8, A = 30° and an arm a of 5, the angle drawn at the first landing is 53.1°

The second answer is found by subtracting the first answer from 180°; if the angles in the triangle do not exceed the angle sum of a triangle, 180°, the second answer can exist: at every arm length from 2 to 9 on the swing-arm screen, a second triangle is drawn exactly when 30° plus 180° minus the first angle B is under 180°, its angle B is 180° minus the first, both landings lie on the base line exactly the arm's length from C, and an arm shorter than the height, 4, lands nowhere

A height dropped from B is found twice: on the height screen, the drawn height, measured off the drawing, equals c sin A and a sin C, with c, a and the angles A and C measured off the same drawing, so a ÷ sin A = c ÷ sin C there too

Every worked number matches the lesson: c = 5 at 90°; 6.08 and 37 at 120°; 3.61 and 13 at 60°, with slips 19 and 0.5; cos 110° = −0.342, a correction of 8.21, c² = 33.21 and c = 5.76, with slips 4.10 and 1.56; 7 laid flat and 1 folded; −0.458 and 117.3° from 3, 4 and 6; 60°, 120° and 38.2° from 5, 8 and 7; 6.74, 3.71 and 7.5; a height of 4, 0.8, 53.1° and 126.9°; 0.667, 41.8°, 138.2° and 318.2°; 73.5, 62.5 and 49.0 nautical miles; 0.161, 9.2° and 170.8°
